newsitem.title: USA: Both Cablevision, TCI to benefit.
newsitem.headline: Both Cablevision, TCI to benefit.

text.p: Cablevision Systems Corp's deal to buy Tele-Communications Inc's New York-area cable business should be a boon to both companies, analysts said Monday.
Cablevision fills holes in its New York operation and acquires valuable annual cash flow, and TCI gets a one-third stake in Cablevision.
"It's a good deal all the way around, a win-win," said Chris Dixon, an analyst at PaineWebber.

Cablevision, a major New York area operator, will buy 10 systems serving 820,000 customers in Rockland and Westchester, N.Y., Long Island and New Jersey in exchange for about 12.2 million Class A shares, or 33 percent of total shares out.
Wall Street gave its approval, sending Cablevision Class A shares soaring $8 to 42-5/8. TCI added one to 16-1/16.
Dixon sees Cablevision at $48 per share and repeated an attractive rating on the stock.
Analysts are looking closely at several aspects of the deal, including the estimated price per cable subscriber that TCI received, and the estimated cash flow.
Analysts said cable TV subscribers have been historically valued at about $1,800-$2,000 per subscriber, with New York at the higher end.
Analysts estimated Cablevision was paying only about $1,300 per subscriber, based on estimated annual cash flow of $200 million a year, and the assumption of $669 million in TCI debt.

While it might appear that TCI was selling at a low price, analysts said, it would benefit through its stake in Cablevision, expecially as Cablevision stock rose sharply from the Friday closing price of 34-5/8.
Analysts said the terms of the deal indicated that TCI put a private market value of at least $80 per Cablevision share.
"The deal validates the higher (price) for Cablevision," said David Doft at Furman Selz.
Cable TV has long been considered among the most leveraged industries, and Cablevision was one of the more leveraged companies, Doft said.

The deal will cut Cablevision's debt to cash flow ratio significantly -- from 8.5 to one to less than seven to one as Cablevision will add $200 million of incremental cash flow from the new subscribers, a move cheered by Wall Street.
"It's highly likely they can grow that cash flow," Dixon said, adding that the new systems will help Cablevision operate more economically.

"It's a phenomenal deal for both companies," said money manager Mario Gabelli, whose funds owned about 3.8 million Cablevision Class A shares at the end of March. He said his firm was buying more stock.
While TCI, the nation's largest cable operator, will also get two seats on Cablevision's board and the one-third stake, the Dolan family will still retain voting control of company.

The Dolan family owns all of the Class B supervoting common shares and currently controls 85-90 percent of the company's total voting power. Charles Dolan is chairman and James Dolan is chief executive officer.
